questions.question: An oscilloscope time-base is set to 2.0 ms per division. One complete cycle of the trace spans 5.0 divisions of the screen. What is the frequency of the signal? A 0.10 Hz, B 100 Hz, C 200 Hz, D 500 Hz
questions.answer: B: 100 Hz
steps: Period T = 5.0 divisions x 2.0 ms per division = 10 ms = 0.010 s.
A does not convert ms to s (1 / 10); C uses 1 / 5.0 ms; D uses 1 / 2.0 ms, the time for one division.

questions.question: Two points P and Q lie on a progressive wave of wavelength 0.60 m. They are 0.15 m apart along the direction of travel of the wave. What is the phase difference between the oscillations at P and Q? A pi/4 rad, B pi rad, C pi/2 rad, D 3pi/2 rad
questions.answer: C: pi/2 rad
steps: Phase difference = 2 pi x (separation / wavelength) = 2 pi x 0.15 / 0.60 = pi/2 rad (1.57 rad).
A has forgotten the factor of 2 (pi x 0.25); B is the phase difference for a separation of lambda/2; D is for a separation of 3 lambda/4.

questions.question: Describe the difference between a transverse wave and a longitudinal wave, and give one example of each.
questions.answer: In a transverse wave the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer; in a longitudinal wave they are parallel to it. Example of transverse: light (or water ripples). Example of longitudinal: sound.
steps: Transverse wave: the oscillations are at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
Longitudinal wave: the oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer (compressions and rarefactions).
A correct example of each, such as light or water waves (transverse) and sound (longitudinal).
accept: Further transverse examples: any electromagnetic wave, a wave on a rope or string.
Further longitudinal examples: a compression wave along a slinky spring, ultrasound.
Only transverse waves can be polarised.

questions.question: A ship sends a pulse of sound vertically downwards from the surface of the sea. The echo from the sea bed returns after 0.48 s. The speed of sound in sea water is 1.5 x 10^3 m s^-1. Calculate the depth of the sea bed.
questions.answer: Depth = 3.6 x 10^2 m
steps: The pulse travels down and back, so the total distance travelled = v t = 1.5 x 10^3 x 0.48 = 720 m.
The depth is half of this distance: d = v t / 2.

questions.question: A microphone detects a note from a loudspeaker and its signal is displayed on an oscilloscope with a time-base of 0.50 ms per division. Two successive peaks of the trace are 3.6 divisions apart. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s^-1. Determine the wavelength of the sound.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 0.61 m
steps: Frequency f = 1 / T = 1 / 1.8 x 10^-3 = 556 Hz.
v = f lambda, so lambda = v / f = 340 / 556.
lambda = 0.61 m.

questions.question: A signal generator drives a loudspeaker at a frequency of 2.50 kHz. The signal from the generator is displayed on an oscilloscope, together with the signal from a microphone placed in front of the loudspeaker. The microphone is moved slowly away from the loudspeaker along a straight line. Describe what is seen on the oscilloscope each time the microphone moves a distance of one wavelength.
questions.answer: The microphone trace moves relative to the generator trace and comes back into step with it: the two traces are in phase again each time the microphone moves a distance of one wavelength.
steps: The microphone trace moves relative to the generator trace as the microphone moves (the phase difference changes continuously).
The two traces are back in phase (in step, peaks aligned) each time the microphone has moved one wavelength.
accept: The traces are in antiphase when the microphone has moved half a wavelength from an in-phase position.
The phase difference changes by 2 pi rad for each wavelength moved.
The traces have the same frequency, so only their relative positions change.

questions.question: A signal generator drives a loudspeaker at a frequency of 2.50 kHz. A microphone is moved away from the loudspeaker, and its signal is compared on an oscilloscope with the signal from the generator. The traces are in phase at the starting position. The microphone is moved until the traces have been back in phase 10 times. The microphone has then moved 1.36 m. Calculate the speed of sound in air.
questions.answer: Speed of sound = 340 m s^-1 (about 3.4 x 10^2 m s^-1)
steps: The traces are in phase at the start and are in phase again after each further wavelength, so 10 in-phase positions after the start means a distance of 10 wavelengths: lambda = 1.36 / 10 = 0.136 m.
v = f lambda = 2500 x 0.136.

questions.question: In an experiment to measure the speed of sound, a microphone is moved away from a loudspeaker, driven at 2.50 kHz, through 10 wavelengths. The distance moved is 1.36 m, measured with a metre rule to within +/- 0.005 m. Explain why moving the microphone through 10 wavelengths gives a more precise value for the wavelength than moving it through one wavelength. Support your answer with calculations of the percentage uncertainty.
questions.answer: The same absolute uncertainty is a much smaller fraction of a longer distance: about 0.4% for 1.36 m (10 wavelengths) compared with about 3.7% for one wavelength (0.136 m).
steps: Percentage uncertainty in one wavelength = 0.005 / 0.136 x 100 = 3.7%.
Percentage uncertainty in 10 wavelengths = 0.005 / 1.36 x 100 = 0.37%.
The same absolute uncertainty is a smaller percentage of the larger distance, so dividing by 10 gives a more precise wavelength (and speed).
accept: The uncertainty in the wavelength is 0.005 / 10 = 0.0005 m when 10 wavelengths are measured.
A larger number of wavelengths reduces the percentage uncertainty in the speed of sound.
Averaging over many wavelengths reduces the effect of the reading error at the start and end positions.

questions.question: In a double-slit experiment with a laser, the fringe spacing on the screen is w. The slit separation is halved and the distance from the slits to the screen is doubled. What is the new fringe spacing? A w/4, B w, C 2w, D 4w
questions.answer: D: 4w
steps: Fringe spacing w = lambda D / s, so w is proportional to D / s.
Doubling D multiplies w by 2 and halving s multiplies w by a further 2, so the new spacing is 4w.
A inverts both changes, B assumes the changes cancel, C counts only one of them.

questions.question: A stretched string of length 1.20 m is fixed at both ends and vibrates in a stationary wave pattern with three loops. What is the wavelength of the waves on the string? A 0.80 m, B 0.40 m, C 1.2 m, D 2.4 m
steps: Each loop is half a wavelength, so three loops are 3 lambda / 2 = 1.20 m.
B treats each loop as a whole wavelength; C and D are the wavelengths for two loops and for a single loop (the fundamental).

questions.question: State the conditions necessary for two sources of light to be coherent. Explain why two separate filament lamps do not produce an observable interference pattern.
questions.answer: Coherent sources have the same frequency (wavelength) and a constant phase difference. Two filament lamps emit light in short random wave trains, so the phase difference between them changes rapidly and randomly and no stable pattern forms.
steps: Coherent sources have the same frequency (or wavelength).
Coherent sources have a constant (fixed) phase difference.
Separate filament lamps emit light as short random wave trains, so the phase difference between them changes randomly and rapidly and no stable pattern forms.
accept: Light is emitted by many atoms independently, so there is no fixed phase relationship between the lamps.
Any fringes would shift too rapidly to be seen, so the intensity appears uniform.
Coherent light can be obtained by splitting one source into two (for example with a double slit) or by using a laser.

questions.question: Two loudspeakers A and B are connected to the same signal generator and emit sound in phase at a frequency of 850 Hz. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s^-1. A microphone at point P is 3.40 m from A and 4.00 m from B. Deduce whether the microphone detects a maximum or a minimum of loudness at P.
questions.answer: Minimum: the path difference of 0.60 m is 1.5 wavelengths, so the sound waves arrive in antiphase.
steps: Wavelength lambda = v / f = 340 / 850 = 0.40 m.
Path difference = 4.00 - 3.40 = 0.60 m = 1.5 lambda.
A path difference of an odd number of half wavelengths (3 lambda / 2) means the waves arrive in antiphase (phase difference 3 pi rad), so they interfere destructively: a minimum.

questions.question: Light of wavelength 589 nm passes through two narrow parallel slits that are 0.450 mm apart. An interference pattern forms on a screen 1.80 m from the slits. Calculate the separation of adjacent bright fringes on the screen.
questions.answer: Fringe separation = 2.36 x 10^-3 m
steps: Fringe separation w = lambda D / s.
Convert the data: lambda = 589 x 10^-9 m, s = 0.450 x 10^-3 m.

questions.question: A pipe of length 0.45 m is closed at one end and open at the other. A loudspeaker near the open end produces sound of gradually increasing frequency. The speed of sound in air is 340 m s^-1. Ignore end corrections. Calculate the two lowest frequencies at which the air column in the pipe resonates.
questions.answer: Lowest frequency = 189 Hz; next frequency = 567 Hz
steps: There is a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end.
Lowest frequency: L = lambda / 4, so lambda = 4 x 0.45 = 1.80 m and f = v / lambda = 340 / 1.80 = 189 Hz.
Next resonance: L = 3 lambda / 4, so lambda = 0.600 m.
f = 340 / 0.600 = 567 Hz (three times the lowest frequency).

questions.question: A string of length 0.800 m is stretched between two fixed points. The tension in the string is 36 N and its mass per unit length is 6.25 x 10^-4 kg m^-1. The string is plucked at its centre. Explain how a stationary wave is formed on the string.
questions.answer: The wave travelling along the string reflects at the fixed ends. The incident and reflected waves (same frequency and amplitude) travelling in opposite directions superpose to give nodes and antinodes.
steps: The wave travelling along the string is reflected at the fixed ends.
The incident and reflected waves (same frequency and wavelength, travelling in opposite directions) superpose.

At nodes the waves are always in antiphase (destructive interference, no movement); at antinodes they are in phase (constructive interference, maximum amplitude), giving a pattern that does not travel along the string.
accept: There is a node at each fixed end.
Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart.
A stationary wave does not transfer energy along the string.

questions.question: A string of length 0.800 m is stretched between two fixed points. The tension in the string is 36 N and its mass per unit length is 6.25 x 10^-4 kg m^-1. Calculate the speed of transverse waves on the string and the lowest frequency at which a stationary wave can be set up on it.
questions.answer: Wave speed = 240 m s^-1; lowest frequency = 150 Hz
steps: For the lowest frequency there is one loop, so L = lambda / 2 and lambda = 2 x 0.800 = 1.60 m.

questions.question: A string of length 0.800 m and mass per unit length 6.25 x 10^-4 kg m^-1 is stretched between two fixed points. The tension in the string is increased from 36 N to 64 N. Determine the new lowest frequency at which a stationary wave can be set up on the string.
questions.answer: New lowest frequency = 200 Hz
steps: The mass per unit length and the length are unchanged, so the wavelength is still 1.60 m.
New speed v = sqrt(64 / 6.25 x 10^-4) = 320 m s^-1.

questions.question: A ray of light in air is incident on a glass block of refractive index 1.52 at an angle of incidence of 40 degrees. What is the angle of refraction in the glass? A 26 degrees, B 78 degrees, C 25 degrees, D 65 degrees
questions.answer: C: 25 degrees
steps: Snell's law: sin i = n sin r, so sin r = sin 40 / 1.52 = 0.423.
r = 25.0 degrees, so about 25 degrees.
A divides the angle itself by n; B uses sin r = n sin i; D is 90 - 25, the angle between the ray and the surface.

questions.question: The critical angle for light travelling from a liquid into air is 48.0 degrees. What is the refractive index of the liquid? A 1.35, B 0.743, C 1.11, D 1.49
steps: At the critical angle the angle of refraction in air is 90 degrees, so n sin C = 1 x sin 90.
B is sin C, C is tan C and D is 1 / cos C.

questions.question: Unpolarised light from a lamp passes through a polarising filter and then through a second polarising filter. As the second filter is rotated, the intensity of the transmitted light changes from a maximum to zero and back to a maximum. Explain what these observations show about the nature of light.
questions.answer: Light is a transverse wave. The first filter passes only oscillations in one plane; the second passes none of this light when its transmission direction is at 90 degrees to the first, so the light must be plane polarised, which only transverse waves can be.
steps: The first filter transmits only the oscillations in one plane, so the light that emerges is plane polarised.
The second filter transmits no light when its transmission direction is at 90 degrees to that of the first (and a maximum when they are parallel).
Only transverse waves can be polarised, so light is a transverse wave.
accept: Longitudinal waves such as sound cannot be polarised.
The intensity goes from maximum to zero twice in one full rotation of the second filter.
The oscillations of light are at right angles to its direction of travel.

questions.question: State two conditions that must be met for total internal reflection to occur at a boundary between two transparent media. Calculate the critical angle for light travelling from glass of refractive index 1.62 into air.
questions.answer: Conditions: light travels from a medium of higher refractive index to one of lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle. Critical angle = 38.1 degrees
steps: Condition 1: the light travels from the optically denser medium (higher refractive index) towards the less dense medium.
Condition 2: the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle.
At the critical angle the angle of refraction is 90 degrees, so n sin C = 1 and sin C = 1 / 1.62 = 0.617.
C = 38.1 degrees.
accept: The critical angle is the angle of incidence that gives an angle of refraction of 90 degrees.
The light travels from glass to air (a medium of smaller refractive index).
C = 38 degrees to two significant figures.

questions.question: Monochromatic light passes through a single narrow slit and forms a pattern on a distant screen. State how the width of the central bright fringe changes when the slit is made narrower, and explain why.
questions.answer: The central bright fringe becomes wider, because the narrower the gap the more the waves diffract (spread out) as the gap width gets closer to the wavelength.
steps: The central bright fringe becomes wider.
Diffraction (spreading of the waves) is greater when the width of the gap is closer to the wavelength of the light.
A narrower slit spreads the light through a larger angle, so the central maximum is wider.
accept: The central maximum also becomes less bright because less light passes through the slit.
The angle of the first minimum is given by sin theta = lambda / slit width, so a smaller width gives a larger angle.
The width of the central maximum is inversely proportional to the slit width.

questions.question: Light from a laser is directed at right angles to a diffraction grating that has 300 lines per mm. A screen is placed 2.00 m from the grating. The first-order maxima are 0.398 m either side of the central maximum. Show that the angle between the central maximum and a first-order maximum is about 11 degrees.
questions.answer: tan theta = 0.398 / 2.00, so theta = 11.3 degrees, about 11 degrees.
steps: The screen is perpendicular to the central beam, so tan theta = 0.398 / 2.00 = 0.199.
theta = 11.3 degrees, which is about 11 degrees.

questions.question: Light from a laser is directed at right angles to a diffraction grating that has 300 lines per mm. A screen is placed 2.00 m from the grating, and the first-order maxima are 0.398 m either side of the central maximum. Calculate the wavelength of the light from the laser.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 6.51 x 10^-7 m (651 nm)
steps: Grating spacing d = 1 / (300 x 10^3) = 3.33 x 10^-6 m, and tan theta = 0.398 / 2.00 gives theta = 11.25 degrees (use the unrounded angle: 11 degrees would give 636 nm).
n lambda = d sin theta with n = 1, so lambda = 3.33 x 10^-6 x sin(11.25 degrees) = 3.33 x 10^-6 x 0.1952.
lambda = 6.51 x 10^-7 m, i.e. 651 nm.

questions.question: Light from a laser is directed at right angles to a diffraction grating that has 300 lines per mm. Using the wavelength of 651 nm found in part (b), determine the highest order of maximum that can be observed.
questions.answer: Highest order = 5 (sin theta cannot exceed 1, so n <= d / lambda = 5.12)
steps: The maximum possible value of sin theta is 1, so n lambda <= d.
n must be a whole number, so the highest order is 5.

questions.question: What is the energy of a photon of wavelength 500 nm? A 3.98 x 10^-28 J, B 1.33 x 10^-27 J, C 2.49 x 10^-19 J, D 3.98 x 10^-19 J
steps: A does not convert nm to m; B is h / lambda, the momentum of the photon, not its energy; C is the energy in eV (2.49 eV) with a power of ten attached.

questions.question: An electron and a proton are each accelerated from rest through the same potential difference. What is the approximate value of (de Broglie wavelength of the electron) / (de Broglie wavelength of the proton)? A 0.023, B 43, C 1.0, D 1800
steps: Both gain the same kinetic energy E_k = e V. Since p = sqrt(2 m E_k), p is proportional to sqrt(m).
lambda = h / p, so lambda_e / lambda_p = sqrt(m_p / m_e) = sqrt(1.67 x 10^-27 / 9.11 x 10^-31) = 43.
A is the inverse; C would need equal momenta; D is m_p / m_e, which comes from assuming equal speeds.

questions.question: Light of frequency below the threshold frequency of a zinc plate does not cause photoelectric emission, however intense the light is. Explain this observation using the photon model of light.
questions.answer: Each electron absorbs a single photon of energy hf. If hf is less than the work function no electron gains enough energy to escape, and a greater intensity only gives more photons per second, not more energy per photon.
steps: Light consists of photons, each with energy E = h f, and one electron interacts with one photon.
Below the threshold frequency the photon energy is less than the work function (h f < phi), so an electron cannot escape from the surface.
Increasing the intensity only increases the number of photons per second, not the energy of each photon, and electrons cannot build up energy from several photons, so there is still no emission.
accept: Wave theory predicts that energy would build up over time and release electrons, which is not observed.
No emission occurs even after a long exposure time.
The work function is the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface.

questions.question: The work function of a metal is 2.20 eV. Light of wavelength 450 nm is incident on its surface. Calculate (i) the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons, in joules, and (ii) the stopping potential.
questions.answer: (i) Maximum kinetic energy = 9.0 x 10^-20 J; (ii) stopping potential = 0.56 V

questions.question: Two of the energy levels of a hydrogen atom are -3.40 eV and -1.51 eV. An electron makes a transition from the -1.51 eV level to the -3.40 eV level and a photon is emitted. Calculate the wavelength of the photon.
questions.answer: Wavelength = 6.58 x 10^-7 m (658 nm)
steps: E = h c / lambda, so lambda = h c / E.

questions.question: Electrons are accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 850 V in a vacuum. The electrons then pass through a thin sheet of graphite and produce a pattern of rings on a fluorescent screen. Show that the speed of the electrons as they reach the graphite is about 1.7 x 10^7 m s^-1.
questions.answer: v = 1.73 x 10^7 m s^-1, which is about 1.7 x 10^7 m s^-1.
steps: Gain in kinetic energy = e V: 1/2 m v^2 = 1.60 x 10^-19 x 850 = 1.36 x 10^-16 J.

questions.question: Electrons accelerated from rest through a potential difference of 850 V travel at a speed of 1.73 x 10^7 m s^-1 towards a thin sheet of graphite. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons.
questions.answer: de Broglie wavelength = 4.2 x 10^-11 m
steps: lambda = 4.2 x 10^-11 m.

questions.question: Electrons accelerated through a potential difference pass through a thin sheet of graphite and produce a pattern of rings on a fluorescent screen. The accelerating potential difference is increased. Explain what happens to the radius of the rings on the screen, and why the pattern provides evidence for the wave nature of electrons.
questions.answer: The rings get smaller. A greater speed means a greater momentum and a shorter wavelength, so there is less diffraction. A diffraction pattern is produced only by waves, so electrons show wave behaviour.
steps: A greater potential difference gives the electrons a greater speed and so a greater momentum (shorter de Broglie wavelength, lambda = h / p).
A shorter wavelength means less diffraction (smaller angle, sin theta = n lambda / d), so the rings have a smaller radius.
A diffraction pattern is produced only by waves, so electrons show wave behaviour (wave-particle duality).
accept: The rings are produced by the electrons diffracting from the regular spacing of the carbon atoms in graphite.
The kinetic energy of the electrons, e V, increases.
A particle-only model cannot explain a diffraction or interference pattern.
